clinicalPearls: Rare inherited platelet disorder defined by absent or markedly reduced alpha-granules, producing large, agranular platelets that appear pale grey on a Romanowsky-stained film.

Most cases are autosomal recessive due to biallelic NBEAL2 mutations; the platelets fail to package alpha-granule cargo such as von Willebrand factor, fibrinogen, platelet factor 4 and thrombospondin.
Presents with lifelong mild-to-moderate mucocutaneous bleeding, easy bruising, epistaxis and menorrhagia, with excessive bleeding at surgery or childbirth.
Thrombocytopenia is usually mild to moderate and tends to worsen slowly over decades; platelets are characteristically enlarged.
Progressive myelofibrosis and splenomegaly are recognised evolving features, thought to reflect leakage of granule contents and growth factors into the marrow.
The blood film is the key diagnostic clue, and low serum vitamin B12 or elevated levels of granule-derived proteins may be seen; electron microscopy confirms alpha-granule deficiency.
Autosomal dominant forms linked to GFI1B and other genes exist and may show additional red-cell or granulocyte abnormalities.
Management is supportive with antifibrinolytics, hormonal control of menorrhagia and judicious platelet transfusion for major bleeding or surgery.
reference.pathophysiology: Grey platelet syndrome arises from a failure of megakaryocytes to form and retain functional alpha-granules, the storage organelles that normally concentrate haemostatic and adhesive proteins including von Willebrand factor, fibrinogen, factor V, platelet factor 4, thrombospondin, platelet-derived growth factor and P-selectin. In the classical autosomal recessive form, loss-of-function mutations in NBEAL2 (a BEACH-domain protein essential for granule biogenesis and cargo retention) mean that although some granule proteins are synthesised or endocytosed, they are not stably packaged and are lost, leaving empty vacuoles and agranular platelets that stain pale grey. The consequent deficit in granule release blunts platelet activation, aggregation and the local delivery of adhesive and procoagulant proteins, producing a functional platelet defect superimposed on variable thrombocytopenia caused by ineffective thrombopoiesis and shortened platelet survival. Uncontrolled release of granule-derived growth factors, particularly platelet-derived growth factor and transforming growth factor beta, into the marrow microenvironment is believed to drive the progressive reticulin and collagen fibrosis and splenomegaly that characterise the evolving disease. Autosomal dominant variants, notably those due to GFI1B mutations, disturb megakaryocyte transcriptional programmes and may additionally affect erythropoiesis.
additionalDifferentials: MYH9-related disorders (May-Hegglin anomaly and related conditions)
Congenital amegakaryocytic thrombocytopenia and inherited macrothrombocytopenias
Primary myelofibrosis (when marrow fibrosis dominates the picture)
von Willebrand disease and other inherited platelet function defects
additionalInvestigations: Peripheral blood film review for large agranular grey platelets
Platelet electron microscopy demonstrating absent or reduced alpha-granules
Flow cytometry for granule markers such as P-selectin expression on activation
Bone marrow examination with reticulin staining to assess fibrosis
Targeted or panel genetic testing (NBEAL2, GFI1B and related genes)
Assays of granule-derived proteins and serum vitamin B12
redFlags: Major or life-threatening haemorrhage, including intracranial bleeding after trauma
Rapidly progressive splenomegaly with worsening cytopenias suggesting advancing myelofibrosis
Peripartum or perioperative bleeding requiring urgent haemostatic support
New leucoerythroblastic film or transfusion dependence indicating marrow failure
reference.prognosis: Most patients have a mild to moderate lifelong bleeding tendency compatible with a normal lifespan when haemostasis is supported around surgery and childbirth. The main long-term concerns are slowly progressive thrombocytopenia and myelofibrosis, which in a minority lead to significant splenomegaly and transfusion dependence.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing the large platelets and thrombocytopenia as immune thrombocytopenia and giving unnecessary immunosuppression or splenectomy
Overlooking the grey agranular platelets because automated counters may misclassify or exclude them
Attributing the marrow fibrosis to a primary myeloproliferative disorder rather than the underlying platelet defect
Failing to plan haemostatic cover before elective procedures or delivery
Assuming a normal platelet count excludes a clinically important functional platelet defect
references: Nathan and Oski's Hematology and Oncology of Infancy and Childhood (standard reference)
ISTH guidance on inherited platelet disorders (standard reference)
management: Manage bleeding episodes and cover surgery and childbirth with the antifibrinolytic tranexamic acid and platelet transfusions when needed
Control menorrhagia with antifibrinolytics and hormonal therapy such as a combined oral contraceptive or a levonorgestrel intrauterine system
Avoid aspirin, other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and antiplatelet agents that worsen the bleeding tendency
Give iron replacement for bleeding-related iron-deficiency anaemia and ensure hepatitis B immunisation before transfusion exposure
Monitor with serial full blood counts for progressive thrombocytopenia and periodic assessment for splenomegaly and evolving marrow myelofibrosis
Refer to haematology and reserve splenectomy for severe refractory thrombocytopenia
Offer genetic counselling and family testing for autosomal recessive NBEAL2-related disease
